standing_assumptions:
Setting, notation and standing assumptions, as printed. Every passage was read from the rendered page images. Article pages are those of Political Analysis 31 (2023), with the PDF page in parentheses; the supplement is the publisher's Supporting Information (publisher-supplement.pdf, 5 pp., printed and PDF page numbers coincide).
[Notation: Section 2, p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] “Before we proceed, we introduce some notation. Let $n$ be the number of observations. Let $k$ be the number of variables (columns) in the dataset. Let $M_{ij}$ be a random indicator variable for whether or not the $j$th variable in the $i$th row is missing. For notational convenience, we will let $\mathbf{M}_{ij}$ represent the random vector collecting the missingness indicators up to variable $j$ $(M_{i1}, M_{i2}, \ldots, M_{ij})$.”
[Assumption 1, p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] “All rows of the data $((M_{11}, \ldots, M_{1k}), \ldots, (M_{n1}, \ldots, M_{nk}))$ are mutually independent.”
[Assumption 2, p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] “There exists a $q_* \in [0,1)$ such that for all $i$, • $\Pr(M_{i1} = 0) \leq q_*$ and • $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0|\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = 0) \leq q_*$, for all $j \in \{2, \ldots, k\}$ such that $\Pr(\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = 0) > 0$.”
[The quantity $p_{all}$: Section 2.1, p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] “We begin by application of elementary probability theory to yield the following finite-$n$ result. In words, this result establishes an exact lower bound on the probability that all rows of the data will suffer from some missingness. In such instances, listwise deletion would yield no usable data.” Lemma 3 then names $p_{all}$ as “the probability that listwise deletion removes all rows”.
[The sequence: pp. 150-151 (PDF pp. 2-3)] “We can now consider the asymptotic properties of listwise deletion, letting both $k$ and $n$ tend to infinity. To do so, we embed the above problem into a sequence. We let $k_n = f(n)$, where $f$ has range over the natural numbers, and allow $M_{ij,n}$ and therefore $q_{ij,n}$ to vary at each $n$. To ease exposition, we omit notational dependence on $n$.”
[Assumption 4, p. 151 (PDF p. 3)] “The number of covariates grows superlogarithmically in $n$, so that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{f(n)}{log(n)} = \infty$.” The next sentence: “Assumption 4 can be equivalently written in asymptotic shorthand notation as $k = \omega(\log n)$.”
[Reading fixed by the printed text and used in every target] $M_{ij} = 1$ means that entry $(i,j)$ is missing and $M_{ij} = 0$ that it is observed (the proof of Lemma 3, p. 154, treats $1 - \Pr(\mathbf{M}_{ik} = 0)$ as “the probability of a single observation containing at least one missing entry”). The event written $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = 0$ is $\{M_{i1} = \cdots = M_{ij} = 0\}$. Row $i$ is removed by listwise deletion when at least one of $M_{i1}, \ldots, M_{ik}$ equals 1, and $p_{all}$ is the probability that every one of the $n$ rows has at least one $j$ with $M_{ij} = 1$. $q_*$ is an upper bound on a probability of being observed. It is one constant, the same for every row and, along the sequence, for every $n$; the laws of the $M_{ij,n}$ may change with $n$ (this is the reading the validator fixed for P007-N002, which was not confirmed as an error). $n \geq 1$ and $k \geq 1$ are integers; $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The symbol $q_{ij}$ is defined only inside the proof of Lemma 3 (p. 154).
[Supplement, Supporting Information A, p. 1] “Here we demonstrate the finite-$n$ implications of our findings. In the following figures, we plot figures for different values of an upper bound on the conditional probability of each data entry being observed $q_*$, the number of observations (rows) $n$, the number of variables (columns) $k$ and a sharp lower bound on $p_{all}$ denoted $\underline{p_{all}} = (1 - q_*^{f(n)})^n$. $\underline{p_{all}}$ is the lowest possible (”best-case”) probability that listwise deletion removes all data.” And, same page: “By Lemma 3, we can compute $\underline{p_{all}} = (1 - q_*^k)^n$.”
[Supplement, Supporting Information B, p. 3] “Let $n$ be the number of observations. Let $g$ be the number of variable groups in the dataset, within which all observations share an identical missingness pattern. We let $M_{ij}$ be a random indicator variable for whether or not the $j$th group in the $i$th row is missing. We use one indicator for each group due to the shared missingness. Similar to the previous setting, we use $\mathbf{M}_{ij}$ to represent the random vector collecting the missingness indicators up to variable $j$, $(M_{i1}, M_{i2}, \ldots, M_{ij})$. Let $k$ be the number of variables in the dataset. Note that, by construction, we know that $k \geq g$ since groups contain at least one variable.” [p. 4] Assumption 6: “All rows of the data $\left((M_{11}, ..., M_{1g}), ..., (M_{n1}, ..., M_{ng})\right)$ are mutually independent.” Assumption 7: “There exists a $q_* \in [0,1)$ such that for all $i$, • $\Pr(M_{i1} = 0) \leq q_*$ • $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0|\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = \mathbf{0}) \leq q_*$, for all $j \in \{2, \ldots, g\}$ such that $\Pr(\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = \mathbf{0}) > 0$”. The sequence: “Similarly, we will embed the problem into a sequence $g_n = l(n)$, where $l$ has range over the natural numbers, and allow $M_{ij,n}$ and $q_{ij,n}$ to vary at each $n$. We omit the $n$ notation for simplicity.” Assumption 9: “The number of groups of covariates grows superlogarithmically in $n$, so that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{l(n)}{log(n)} = \infty$.”
[Application: Section 3, pp. 151-152 (PDF pp. 3-4)] “We applied mild preprocessing to these datasets: we removed country code variables, and in the case of the State Failure data, to apply the principle of charity, we removed 19 variables that exhibited 100% missingness.” [Section 3.1, p. 152 (PDF p. 4)] “To do so, we conducted 25,000 simulations in each of which we drew $k$ of the variables from each dataset (without replacement). We then recorded the number of rows of the data that survive listwise deletion. We then report the expected proportion of remaining data observed after listwise deletion, as well as the probability that all rows of the data exhibit some missingness. Note that, here, expected values and probabilities refer to the randomness induced by our random subsampling procedure, not any fundamental stochasticity giving rise to the underlying data.” So in the application the data are a fixed array of missing and observed cells, and the only randomness is the uniform draw of $k$ of its variables without replacement. Assumptions 1 and 2 play no part in the targets about the application (P007-T1, P007-T2, P007-T12, P007-T13).
Scope of the targets. Headline claims that are mathematical statements: P007-H1 (Lemma 3: P007-T14), P007-H2 (Proposition 5: P007-T16) and P007-H6 (Lemma 8 and Proposition 10: P007-T15 and P007-T17). P007-H3 (the finite-$n$ illustration of the bound), P007-H4 and P007-H5 (the two data illustrations) and P007-H7 (the conclusion) are numerical illustrations, simulation results or interpretive remarks, so they are not headline targets; the formal content of the findings that touch P007-H3 and P007-H5 is in the targets below. Confirmed errors with mathematical content, each with a corrected-statement target: P007-E010 (Moderate; Table 1's State Failure average and the threshold “more than three variables”: exact refutation P007-T1, correction P007-T2, statement as printed P007-T13); P007-E003 (Minor; the printed proofs of Lemmas 3 and 8 and of Propositions 5 and 10: P007-T3 to P007-T6); P007-E005 (Minor; the Figure 4 paragraph of the supplement: P007-T7, P007-T8); P007-E006 (Minor; “upper bound” and the caption of Figure 5: P007-T9, P007-T10); P007-E004 (Minor; “i.i.d.” for Assumption 1: P007-T11); P007-E014 (Minor; its established part is the same stale Table 1 average: P007-T12). Confirmed errors that are not targets, because their corrections change no mathematical statement: P007-E009 (Moderate; the analysed file is the QoG Basic dataset and not the Standard dataset that is cited, a matter of data provenance, and every QoG number stands for the deposited file); P007-E001 (the glmnet software example); P007-E013 (a garbled reference entry); within P007-E004, the misprint “out” for “our”; within P007-E014, the behaviour of the is.na mask on empty Stata strings (a property of the code whose effect on the State Failure data was not established). Not targets because they are not rated as errors: P007-E002 and P007-N001 (clarity notes), P007-N002, P007-N004, P007-N005 and P007-N006 (not confirmed), P007-N003 (undetermined), P007-N007 (out of scope).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.2, State Failure paragraph, last sentence (“With more than three variables, the loss is more than 99%”), read with Table 1 and Section 3.1. The refutation is the validator's exact bound and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 153 (PDF p. 5), Section 3.2, third paragraph; Table 1 and Section 3.1, p. 152 (PDF p. 4)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 153 (PDF p. 5)] “We found similar, but more dramatic, trends with the State Failure dataset. The left panel of Figure 2 plots the expected proportion of observed data against the number of randomly selected variables for the State Failure dataset. The proportion decreases at a faster rate compared with the QoG dataset. The researcher can expect to lose more than 50% of the data if the only variable included is randomly selected. With more than three variables, the loss is more than 99%.” [Printed, Table 1, p. 152 (PDF p. 4), State Failure column] Number of observations: 8,580. Number of variables: 1,205.
[Exact refutation of the last sentence at four variables. The argument is the validator's and is not in the paper.] Let $n = 8580$ and $K = 1205$, and let $m \in \{0,1\}^{n \times K}$ be any fixed array ($m_{ij} = 1$: cell $(i,j)$ is missing; $m_{ij} = 0$: it is observed). For each row $i$ let $r_i = \#\{j : m_{ij} = 0\}$ be its number of observed cells, so that $r_i$ is an integer with $0 \leq r_i \leq 1205$. Let $S$ be uniformly distributed over the $\binom{1205}{4}$ sets of four distinct columns (the draw of $k = 4$ variables without replacement of Section 3.1), and let $\rho_4(S) = \frac{1}{n}\,\#\{i : m_{ij} = 0 \text{ for all } j \in S\}$ be the proportion of rows that survive listwise deletion on the selected variables.
(i) [Counting identity] $\mathrm{E}[\rho_4(S)] = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\binom{r_i}{4}}{n\binom{1205}{4}}$, where $\binom{r}{4} = 0$ for $r < 4$. Nothing is assumed about dependence between rows or between columns.
(ii) [Supporting line] For every integer $r$ with $0 \leq r \leq 1205$, $\binom{r}{4} \geq \binom{405}{4} + (r - 405)\binom{405}{3} = 1104475905 + 10989810\,(r - 405)$, with equality at $r = 405$ and at $r = 406$ ($\binom{406}{4} = 1115465715$).
(iii) [Bound on the numerator] If the total number of observed cells is $\sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i = 3482533$ (which equals $8580 \cdot 405 + 7633$; this is the total implied by the authors' log, see definitions_needed), then $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\binom{r_i}{4} \geq 947\binom{405}{4} + 7633\binom{406}{4} = 9560288484630$, where $947 = 8580 - 7633$.
(iv) [Denominator] $8580 \cdot \binom{1205}{4} = 749997256908900$.
(v) [Conclusion] Under the hypothesis of (iii), $\mathrm{E}[\rho_4(S)] \geq \dfrac{9560288484630}{749997256908900} = \dfrac{24513560217}{1923069889510} > \dfrac{1}{100}$. So the expected proportion of rows lost with four randomly selected variables, $1 - \mathrm{E}[\rho_4(S)]$, is at most $\dfrac{1898556329293}{1923069889510} < \dfrac{99}{100}$ (about 98.73%), for every $8580 \times 1205$ array with this number of observed cells. The printed sentence asserts an expected loss of more than 99% for every number of variables greater than three; it is false at $k = 4$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Section 3.1, p. 152 (PDF p. 4)] the simulation draws “$k$ of the variables from each dataset (without replacement)” and reports “the expected proportion of remaining data observed after listwise deletion”, where “expected values and probabilities refer to the randomness induced by our random subsampling procedure”; the “loss” of p. 153 is one minus that expected proportion. [Table 1, p. 152] State Failure: 8,580 observations and 1,205 variables, after the removal of “19 variables that exhibited 100% missingness” (pp. 151-152). [The observed-cell total; not printed in the paper] The authors' log Simcode_Statefailure.Rout prints the Table 1 column with 8580 rows, 1205 variables and “Proportion of Missing Values (Avg)” 0.668390827582004; in Simcode_Statefailure.R that average is computed at lines 28-29, before the 19 entirely missing columns are dropped at lines 39-40, so it is an average over $1224$ columns. P007-T2 (i) derives from it $7019387$ missing cells among $8580 \cdot 1224 = 10501920$, hence $6856367$ missing and $3482533$ observed cells among the $8580 \cdot 1205 = 10338900$ retained.
canonical_claim.note: The kind is counterexample in the sense of an exact refutation: there is no free witness to choose, because the statement holds for every array with the stated dimensions and observed-cell total, the authors' data among them. The validator's evidence is a Lean proof (check.lean, compiled without sorry; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound): supportingLine is (ii) for all 1,206 values of $r$, numeratorLowerBound is (iii), denominatorValue is (iv), and fourVariablesCannotLoseMoreThan99Percent is $8580\binom{1205}{4} < 100\sum_i\binom{r_i}{4}$ for $r : \{1,\ldots,8580\} \to \{0,\ldots,1205\}$ with $\sum_i r_i = 3482533$. It may be reused once checked against this statement. It does not formalize the counting identity (i) or the passage from the log to the total; (i) is part of this target, and the passage from the log is P007-T2 (i). The steps are written out in derivation.md in the same folder (sections 3 and 4). The hypothesis $\sum_i r_i = 3482533$ is inferred from the authors' log, not recounted from the data (sort11v3.dta was not staged for the validators). The bound is deliberately conservative and is not the actual mean: the authors' simulation estimates the retained proportion at four variables as 0.02820753. A check made when this list was fixed, not part of the target: the same argument with only the printed Table 1 as input (average missingness below 66.85%, hence at least 3,427,346 observed cells) gives $\mathrm{E}[\rho_4(S)] > 0.0119 > 0.01$, so the printed sentence is inconsistent with the printed table as well. What is not established: the exact number of variables from which the expected loss exceeds 99%; “six or more” is a statement about the simulation estimates (P007-T2 (iii)). The finding is rated Moderate; the simulation, Figure 2 and the conclusion of rapid loss are unchanged. All integers in the statement were recomputed in exact arithmetic when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Table 1, State Failure column, “Proportion of missing values (avg.)”, and Section 3.2, the sentence “With more than three variables, the loss is more than 99%”, as repaired by Sol
canonical_claim.location: Table 1, p. 152 (PDF p. 4); Section 3.2, third paragraph, p. 153 (PDF p. 5)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] Table 1 (p. 152), State Failure column: “Proportion of missing values (avg.)” 66.8%. Section 3.2 (p. 153): “With more than three variables, the loss is more than 99%.”
[Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P007-E010, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “For the deposited R missingness definition after removing 19 fully missing columns, Table 1 should report 66.3% (6,856,367/10,338,900). In the simulation, the estimated loss exceeds 99% with six or more variables; estimated retained fractions at four, five, and six variables are 0.02820753, 0.01365003, and 0.006640252.” [Sol's smallest repair, the two changes to the article] Change Table 1's State Failure average to 66.3%, and replace the threshold sentence by “In the simulation, the estimated loss exceeds 99% with six or more variables.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis]
(i) [The average] Let $n = 8580$, $K = 1205$, $d = 19$ and $R = K + d = 1224$. Let $A$ be the number of missing cells of the $n \times R$ array before its $d$ entirely missing columns are removed; the average over the $R$ columns of the column missing proportions is then $A/(nR)$, with $nR = 10501920$. Hypothesis, from the authors' log: $\left|A/(nR) - 0.668390827582004\right| \leq 10^{-9}$. Then: (a) $A = 7019387$, the only integer satisfying the hypothesis. (b) Removing the $d$ entirely missing columns removes $nd = 163020$ missing cells and no observed cell, which leaves $A - nd = 6856367$ missing cells among $nK = 10338900$, and $10338900 - 6856367 = 3482533$ observed cells. (c) The average for the 1,205 retained variables is $\frac{6856367}{10338900}$, and $0.6625 \leq \frac{6856367}{10338900} < 0.6635$: it is 66.3% to one decimal place, and it is not 66.8% ($\frac{6856367}{10338900} < 0.6675$). (d) The average before removal, $\frac{7019387}{10501920}$, lies in $[0.6675, 0.6685)$: the printed 66.8% is the average over the 1,224 columns.
(ii) [The threshold: what is exact] For every $8580 \times 1205$ array of missing and observed cells with $3482533$ observed cells, the expected proportion of rows lost when four variables are drawn uniformly without replacement is at most $\frac{1898556329293}{1923069889510} < \frac{99}{100}$ (P007-T1). So an expected loss of more than 99% cannot begin at four variables.
(iii) [The threshold: the simulation estimates] The estimated retained proportions in the authors' log at $k = 4$, $5$ and $6$ variables are $0.02820753$, $0.01365003$ and $0.006640252$, that is, estimated losses of $0.97179247$, $0.98634997$ and $0.993359748$. Since $0.97179247 < 0.98634997 < 0.99 < 0.993359748$, among these estimates the loss first exceeds 99% at six variables.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Table 1, p. 152] “Proportion of missing values (avg.)”: the average over the variables of the proportion of rows in which the variable is missing; every variable has the same $n$ rows, so the average equals the number of missing cells divided by the number of cells. [pp. 151-152] “we removed 19 variables that exhibited 100% missingness”. [Authors' log, Simcode_Statefailure.Rout] the Table 1 column printed by the script: “Number of Observations” 8580, “Number of Variables” 1205, “Proportion of Missing Values (Avg)” 0.668390827582004; and the table expected_table_sf of estimated retained proportions, whose rows for 1, 4, 5 and 6 variables read 3.361604e-01, 2.820753e-02, 1.365003e-02 and 6.640252e-03. [Script, Simcode_Statefailure.R] line 29 assigns prop.missing <- mean(colMeans(isnamatrix)) before the columns of maximum missingness are dropped (lines 39-40); line 55 prints that value beside the retained dimensions. The tolerance $10^{-9}$ is the validators' deliberately loose allowance for floating-point and display error; one cell changes the average by $1/10501920 \approx 9.5 \times 10^{-8}$.
canonical_claim.note: From Sol's smallest_repair and corrected text for P007-E010 and sections 3 to 5 of the validator's derivation. Part (i) is exact arithmetic from the logged decimal: the interval $[nR(t - 10^{-9}),\ nR(t + 10^{-9})]$ with $t = 0.668390827582004$ has endpoints $\frac{10967792171090749137}{1562500000000}$ and $\frac{10967792203909249137}{1562500000000}$, and contains the single integer $7019387$. The counts are inferred from the log; the data file was not staged for the validators, so they are not a recount. That the logged value is the pre-removal average is a fact about the script and not a Lean matter. The identity that links the two averages for any array is P007-T12 (i). Part (iii) is a reading of the authors' archived Monte Carlo estimates (25,000 draws per $k$); the comparisons are trivial arithmetic and say nothing about the exact population expectations, which the validator did not recompute. In the full log every estimate from six to one hundred variables is below 0.01. The preceding printed sentence (“more than 50% of the data if the only variable included is randomly selected”) stands: with one variable the expected loss equals the average missingness, $\frac{6856367}{10338900} > \frac{1}{2}$, and the logged estimate is $1 - 0.3361604 = 0.6638396$. The script-side repair (recompute prop.missing after the final mask is built) is a code change and not a mathematical statement. All numbers were recomputed in exact arithmetic when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Lemma 3, the case $q_* = 0$ (“which is equivalent to say that all variables are fully missing”), and the same step in the Proof of Lemma 8. The witness is the validator's and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 154 (PDF p. 6), Appendix: Proofs, Proof of Lemma 3, first three sentences; Supplement p. 4, Proof of Lemma 8, first three sentences
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 154 (PDF p. 6), Proof of Lemma 3] “We will prove the result in two cases. First suppose $q_* = 0$, which is equivalent to say that all variables are fully missing. Then $p_{all} = 1 = (1 - q_*^k)^n$.” [Printed, Supplement p. 4, Proof of Lemma 8] “Similar to the proof of Lemma 3, we will still consider two cases for $q_*$. Suppose $q_* = 0$. Since this entails that all groups of variables are completely missing, $p_{all} = 1 = (1 - q_*^g)^n$.”
[Counterexample to the assertion that, under Assumptions 1 and 2, $q_* = 0$ is equivalent to (or entails) every variable being missing with probability one. Validator's witness; not in the paper.] Let $n = 1$ and $k = 2$, and let the single row have the law $\Pr(M_{11} = 1,\ M_{12} = 0) = 1$: the first variable is always missing and the second is always observed. Then:
(i) Assumption 1 holds (there is one row).
(ii) Assumption 2 holds with $q_* = 0$: $\Pr(M_{11} = 0) = 0 \leq 0$; and for $j = 2$ the conditioning event has probability $\Pr(\mathbf{M}_{11} = 0) = \Pr(M_{11} = 0) = 0$, so the assumption imposes no condition.
(iii) $\Pr(M_{12} = 0) = 1$ and $\Pr(M_{12} = 1) = 0$: the second variable is observed with probability one, so it is not the case that all variables are fully missing.
(iv) The displayed consequence is unaffected: the row has a missing entry with probability one, so $p_{all} = 1 = (1 - 0^2)^1$.
(v) The other direction of “equivalent” also fails as a statement about $q_*$: for the law $\Pr(M_{11} = 1,\ M_{12} = 1) = 1$ (all variables fully missing), Assumption 2 holds with $q_* = \frac{1}{2}$ as well as with $q_* = 0$, indeed with every $q_* \in [0,1)$, because $\Pr(M_{11} = 0) = 0 \leq q_*$ and the conditioning event for $j = 2$ has probability zero. $q_*$ is an upper bound and not the least one, so full missingness does not make $q_*$ equal to 0.
(vi) Group version: with the two variables read as two groups of one variable each ($g = k = 2$), the law of (i) to (iv) satisfies Assumptions 6 and 7 with $q_* = 0$ while the second group is observed with probability one.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] $n$, the number of observations; $k$, the number of variables (columns); $M_{ij}$, “a random indicator variable for whether or not the $j$th variable in the $i$th row is missing”; $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = (M_{i1}, M_{i2}, \ldots, M_{ij})$, “the random vector collecting the missingness indicators up to variable $j$”; Assumption 1 and Assumption 2 as transcribed in standing_assumptions; $p_{all}$, “the probability that listwise deletion removes all rows” (Lemma 3, p. 150). Reading: $M_{ij} = 1$ missing, $M_{ij} = 0$ observed; $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = 0$ is the event $\{M_{i1} = \cdots = M_{ij} = 0\}$; $p_{all} = \Pr(\text{every row } i \text{ has some } j \text{ with } M_{ij} = 1)$. “Fully missing” (p. 154) and “completely missing” (Supplement p. 4) are not defined in the paper; they are read as $\Pr(M_{ij} = 1) = 1$ for every row $i$ and every variable (group) $j$. For the group version: [Supplement p. 3] $g$, “the number of variable groups in the dataset, within which all observations share an identical missingness pattern”; $M_{ij}$, “a random indicator variable for whether or not the $j$th group in the $i$th row is missing”; $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = (M_{i1}, M_{i2}, \ldots, M_{ij})$ (printed “up to variable $j$”; the indicators are those of groups $1, \ldots, j$); $k$, the number of variables, with $k \geq g$. [Supplement p. 4] Assumptions 6 and 7 as transcribed in standing_assumptions. A row is complete exactly when all $g$ of its group indicators are 0, and $p_{all}$ is the probability that every row has at least one group indicator equal to 1.
canonical_claim.note: Witness A of the validator's derivation (section “Exact witnesses”), checked in exact arithmetic by exact_check.py in the same folder; part (v) is the validator's remark after witness A (its exact_check.txt calls that law witness D). The witness refutes a sentence of the proof, not the lemma: $p_{all} = 1$ at $q_* = 0$ is true, and Lemma 3 and Lemma 8 hold as printed (P007-T14, P007-T15). What is true in general at $q_* = 0$ is P007-T5 (a): the first variable (group) of every row is missing with probability one, and later ones are unrestricted. P007-E003 is rated Minor: after the repair every lemma and proposition holds under the stated assumptions.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Lemma 3, the definition of $q_{ij}$ and the step “By Assumption 2, $q_{ij} \leq q_*$, for all $j \in \{1,2,\ldots,k\}$”, and the same step in the Proof of Lemma 8. The witnesses are the validator's and are not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 154 (PDF p. 6), Appendix: Proofs, Proof of Lemma 3; Supplement p. 4, Proof of Lemma 8
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 154 (PDF p. 6), Proof of Lemma 3] “Now suppose $q_* \in (0,1)$. By the independence assumption, $p_{all} = \Pi_{i=1}^{n}(1 - \Pr(\mathbf{M}_{ik} = 0))$. Denote $q_{ij} = \Pr(M_{ij} = 0|\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = 0)$ if $j > 1$, else $q_{ij} = \Pr(M_{ij} = 0)$. By Assumption 2, $q_{ij} \leq q_*$, for all $j \in \{1,2,\ldots,k\}$. By the chain rule of conditional probability, $\Pr(\mathbf{M}_{ik} = 0) = q_{i1}, q_{i2}, \ldots, q_{ik}$.” [Printed, Supplement p. 4, Proof of Lemma 8] “For the second case suppose $q_* \in (0,1)$. By the group independence assumption, $p_{all} = \Pi_{i=1}^{n}(1 - \Pr(\mathbf{M}_{ig} = \mathbf{0}))$. Denote $q_{ij} = \Pr(M_{ij} = 0|\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = \mathbf{0})$ if $j > 1$, else $q_{ij} = \Pr(M_{ij} = 0)$. By Assumption 7, $q_{ij} \leq q_*$, for all $j \in \{1,2,\ldots,g\}$. By the chain rule of conditional probability, $\Pr(\mathbf{M}_{ig} = \mathbf{0}) = q_{i1}q_{i2} \cdots q_{ig}$.”
[Counterexamples to the step: in the case $q_* \in (0,1)$, under Assumptions 1 and 2, each $q_{ij}$ is a defined conditional probability that Assumption 2 bounds by $q_*$. Validator's witnesses; not in the paper.] Write $s_{ij} = \Pr(M_{i1} = \cdots = M_{ij} = 0)$, so that for $j > 1$ the printed $q_{ij}$ is the ratio $s_{ij}/s_{i(j-1)}$, which is defined when $s_{i(j-1)} > 0$.
Witness B. $n = 1$, $k = 2$, $\Pr(M_{11} = 1,\ M_{12} = 0) = 1$, $q_* = \frac{1}{2}$. (i) Assumptions 1 and 2 hold: $\Pr(M_{11} = 0) = 0 \leq \frac{1}{2}$, and no condition is imposed at $j = 2$ because $s_{11} = 0$. (ii) $s_{11} = 0$ and $s_{12} = 0$: the printed $q_{12}$ is the ratio $0/0$, a conditional probability given an event of probability zero, in the case $q_* \in (0,1)$ of the proof. (iii) Assumption 2 bounds no value that might be assigned to $q_{12}$: every $v \in [0,1]$ satisfies the defining relation $s_{12} = v\, s_{11}$ (it reads $0 = v \cdot 0$), in particular $v = 1 > \frac{1}{2} = q_*$. With $v = 1$ the chain-rule product $q_{11} v = 0 \cdot 1 = 0 = s_{12}$ is correct but the bound $q_{12} \leq q_*$ fails; with $v = 0$ both hold. (iv) The lemma's conclusion still holds: $s_{12} = 0 \leq q_*^2 = \frac{1}{4}$ and $p_{all} = 1 \geq 1 - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}$.
Witness C (a null prefix that does not start at the first variable). $k = 3$, $q_* = \frac{1}{2}$, $n = 2$ independent rows, each with the law $\Pr\big((M_{i1}, M_{i2}, M_{i3}) = (1,0,0)\big) = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\Pr\big((M_{i1}, M_{i2}, M_{i3}) = (0,1,0)\big) = \frac{1}{2}$. (v) Assumptions 1 and 2 hold: $s_{i1} = \frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{1}{2}$; $s_{i1} > 0$ and $\Pr(M_{i2} = 0 \mid M_{i1} = 0) = s_{i2}/s_{i1} = 0 \leq \frac{1}{2}$; $s_{i2} = 0$, so no condition is imposed at $j = 3$. (vi) $q_{i1} = \frac{1}{2}$, $q_{i2} = 0$, and the printed $q_{i3}$ is the ratio $0/0$. (vii) The conclusion holds: $s_{i3} = 0 \leq \frac{1}{8}$ and $p_{all} = 1 \geq \left(1 - \frac{1}{8}\right)^2 = \frac{49}{64}$.
(viii) Group version: the same laws, with each variable read as a group of one variable, satisfy Assumptions 6 and 7 and leave the $q_{i2}$ (witness B) and $q_{i3}$ (witness C) of the proof of Lemma 8 undefined in the same way.

canonical_claim.note: Witnesses B and C of the validator's derivation, checked by exact_check.py in the same folder. The formal content is that every hypothesis holds while a prefix event has probability zero, so that the positive-probability proviso of Assumption 2 leaves the corresponding condition vacuous and the ratio that defines $q_{ij}$ is $0/0$: parts (i) to (iii) and (v) to (vi). It is a gap in the printed proof (an omitted case or convention), not a counterexample to Lemma 3 or Lemma 8, as (iv) and (vii) record; the repair is P007-T5 (b) and (c). Fidelity caution: a formalization in which conditional probability is a total function that takes the value 0 given a null event has already made the repair of P007-T5 (c), and in it the printed inequality would hold trivially (Mathlib's ProbabilityTheory.cond appears to behave in this way; to be confirmed by the formalizer). The target should therefore be stated through the prefix probabilities $s_{ij}$ and the relation $s_{ij} = v\, s_{i(j-1)}$, not through a library convention.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proofs of Lemma 3 and Lemma 8, as repaired (Sol's smallest repair and the validator's derivation). The statements of the two lemmas are unchanged
canonical_claim.location: p. 154 (PDF p. 6), Appendix: Proofs, Proof of Lemma 3; Supplement p. 3 (definition of $\mathbf{M}_{ij}$) and p. 4 (Proof of Lemma 8)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed proof of Lemma 3, p. 154 (PDF p. 6), in full] “We will prove the result in two cases. First suppose $q_* = 0$, which is equivalent to say that all variables are fully missing. Then $p_{all} = 1 = (1 - q_*^k)^n$. Now suppose $q_* \in (0,1)$. By the independence assumption, $p_{all} = \Pi_{i=1}^{n}(1 - \Pr(\mathbf{M}_{ik} = 0))$. Denote $q_{ij} = \Pr(M_{ij} = 0|\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = 0)$ if $j > 1$, else $q_{ij} = \Pr(M_{ij} = 0)$. By Assumption 2, $q_{ij} \leq q_*$, for all $j \in \{1,2,\ldots,k\}$. By the chain rule of conditional probability, $\Pr(\mathbf{M}_{ik} = 0) = q_{i1}, q_{i2}, \ldots, q_{ik}$. This means that the probability of a single observation containing at least one missing entry is $(1 - q_{i1}, q_{i2}, \ldots, q_{ik})$. Since $q_* \geq q_{ij}$ for all $j \in \{1,2,\ldots,k\}$, $q_*^k \geq q_{i1}, q_{i2}, \ldots, q_{ik}$. Thus $(1 - q_*^k) \leq (1 - q_{i1}, q_{i2}, \ldots, q_{ik})$. Thus $(1 - q_*^k)^n$ is a lower bound for the probability of all $n$ observations each containing at least one missing entry.” The proof of Lemma 8 (Supplement p. 4) is the same with $g$ for $k$, Assumption 7 for Assumption 2, “the group independence assumption” for “the independence assumption”, and the products printed as $q_{i1}q_{i2} \cdots q_{ig}$.
[Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P007-E003, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “Main page 154 and supplement pages 3-5: If q_*=0, the first variable/group is missing almost surely in every row, hence p_all=1. Let C_ij be the event that row i survives its first j variables/groups, with C_i0 the sure event. If P(C_i,j-1)=0 then P(C_ij)=0; otherwise Assumption 2/7 gives P(C_ij)<=q_* P(C_i,j-1). Thus P(C_ih)<=q_*^h and row independence gives p_all>=(1-q_*^h)^n, with h=k or g. Bernoulli gives 1-nq_*^h<=(1-q_*^h)^n<=1. For fixed 0<q_*<1 and h/log n tending to infinity, nq_*^h tends to zero; for q_*=0 the endpoint is immediate. Therefore p_all tends to 1. Replace the comma lists with products, remove stars on >=, balance superscript parentheses, write g=l(n) on supplement page 4, and up to group j on supplement page 3. Row independence (Assumption 6) may replace the group independence label for clarity.” The sentences from “Bernoulli gives” to “Therefore p_all tends to 1” concern the propositions and are P007-T6.
[Mathematical content of the repaired lemma proofs, with every hypothesis]
[Setting] Integers $n \geq 1$ and $h \geq 1$, where $h = k$ (the number of variables) for Lemma 3 and $h = g$ (the number of groups) for Lemma 8. A probability space carrying indicators $M_{ij} \in \{0,1\}$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$ and $j = 1, \ldots, h$, with $M_{ij} = 1$ when variable (group) $j$ of row $i$ is missing and $M_{ij} = 0$ when it is observed. For $j = 0, 1, \ldots, h$ let $C_{ij} = \{M_{i1} = \cdots = M_{ij} = 0\}$, with $C_{i0}$ the sure event, and $s_{ij} = \Pr(C_{ij})$; $C_{ij}$ is the printed event $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = 0$, where in the supplement $\mathbf{M}_{ij}$ collects the indicators up to group $j$ (printed: “up to variable $j$”). $p_{all} = \Pr\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{n} C_{ih}^{c}\right)$.
[Hypotheses] (A2: Assumption 2, respectively 7) $q_*$ is a real number in $[0,1)$ such that, for every row $i$: $s_{i1} \leq q_*$, and for every $j \in \{2, \ldots, h\}$ with $s_{i(j-1)} > 0$, $s_{ij}/s_{i(j-1)} \leq q_*$ (the ratio is $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0 \mid \mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = 0)$). (A1: Assumption 1, respectively 6) the $n$ row vectors $(M_{i1}, \ldots, M_{ih})$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, are mutually independent.
[Statement]
(a) [Replaces “$q_* = 0$, which is equivalent to say that all variables are fully missing”.] Under (A2), if $q_* = 0$ then $\Pr(M_{i1} = 1) = 1$ for every row $i$; hence every row has a missing entry with probability one and $p_{all} = 1 = (1 - q_*^h)^n$. Nothing follows about $M_{ij}$ for $j \geq 2$ (P007-T3). Row independence is not used.
(b) [Replaces “By Assumption 2, $q_{ij} \leq q_*$, for all $j$”.] Under (A2), for every row $i$ and every $j \in \{1, \ldots, h\}$: $s_{ij} \leq q_*\, s_{i(j-1)}$. The three cases are: $j = 1$, where $s_{i0} = 1$; $j \geq 2$ with $s_{i(j-1)} = 0$, where $C_{ij} \subseteq C_{i(j-1)}$ gives $s_{ij} = 0$; and $j \geq 2$ with $s_{i(j-1)} > 0$, where (A2) applies.
(c) [Replaces the chain-rule sentence and the comma lists.] Define $q_{i1} = s_{i1}$ and, for $j \geq 2$, $q_{ij} = s_{ij}/s_{i(j-1)}$ if $s_{i(j-1)} > 0$ and $q_{ij} = 0$ if $s_{i(j-1)} = 0$. Then $\Pr(\mathbf{M}_{ih} = 0) = s_{ih} = q_{i1} q_{i2} \cdots q_{ih}$, a product (the printed “$q_{i1}, q_{i2}, \ldots, q_{ik}$” denotes this product); and under (A2), $0 \leq q_{ij} \leq q_*$ for all $j \in \{1, \ldots, h\}$.
(d) Under (A2), $s_{ih} \leq q_*^h$ for every row $i$; equivalently $(1 - q_*^h) \leq (1 - q_{i1} q_{i2} \cdots q_{ih})$: each row contains at least one missing entry with probability at least $1 - q_*^h$.
(e) Under (A1) and (A2), $p_{all} = \prod_{i=1}^{n}(1 - s_{ih}) \geq (1 - q_*^h)^n$, for every $q_* \in [0,1)$ and with no separate case for $q_* = 0$.

canonical_claim.note: From Sol's smallest_repair (“Replace the zero-bound explanation by: the first variable/group is missing almost surely in every row, so p_all=1. For j>1 define q_ij=0 when the all-observed prefix has probability zero and otherwise use the stated conditional probability; alternatively prove the prefix-probability inequality by separate zero/positive-prefix cases. Change the four comma lists to products [...] and change up to variable j to up to group j on supplement page 3”) and from the section “General proof of Lemmas 3 and 8, including all null prefixes” of the validator's derivation. Repair cost: none; no assumption is added and no conclusion is weakened. Parts (b), (d) and (e) are the validator's induction; part (c) is its “even smaller edit” that keeps the printed product. Part (e) with the lemma's statement is P007-T14 (and P007-T15 for groups), so a proof of (a) to (e) proves the two headline lemmas. Two repairs of wording are not mathematical statements and are recorded here only: in the supplement the phrase “By the group independence assumption” refers to Assumption 6, independence across rows (no independence across groups is assumed or used, and the validator did not treat the phrase as an error); and “up to variable $j$” on Supplement p. 3 should read “up to group $j$”. The validator's Lean file for P007-N002 (runs/P007/validate/P007-N002/v1/artifact/check.lean) contains the algebra of (b), (d) and (e) for real sequences (prefix_survival_bound, lemma3_algebra), without the probability space; it may be reused once checked against this statement.
